scenes.title: CloudFormation Dependencies, Outputs and Change Sets
scenes.narration: This diagram explains how CloudFormation decides the order in which resources are created and how an operator reviews changes. Start with the YAML resource definitions. The Lambda function references its IAM role using GetAtt, which creates an implicit dependency: the role needs to exist before CloudFormation can configure the function. References and dependency metadata establish an ordering graph rather than relying on the order the resources appear in the template. The Outputs section publishes selected values such as a bucket name, which other stacks or applications can consume when configured appropriately. Now read the change-set preview. It lists additions, modifications and replacements and can flag that a property change may recreate an S3 bucket or another resource. A change set is only a preview until you execute it. Review replacements carefully because they can cause downtime, endpoint changes or data loss, depending on resource policies and migration procedures. For a production GenAI platform, use change sets to understand the impact of changing a function role, database or data bucket before approving the deployment.

scenes.title: CloudFormation Rollback, Drift and Retention
scenes.narration: The left-hand panel compares a declarative CloudFormation template with resources actually running in AWS. Drift detection identifies supported configuration differences, for example when an operator manually changes a managed resource outside the stack. That produces evidence for review; it does not automatically repair every difference. The next branch explains rollback. If a stack update fails, CloudFormation attempts to return the stack to its previous stable state where supported, but recovery is not always instantaneous or automatic for every resource and failure. The bottom panels separate two data-protection concepts. DeletionPolicy controls what happens when the stack is deleted or a resource is removed from the template. UpdateReplacePolicy controls how the old physical resource is handled when CloudFormation must replace it. Retain can preserve data after a stack change, but also leaves resources that continue generating cost and require ongoing governance. For a GenAI workload, apply retention decisions deliberately to S3 data lakes, databases and KMS-sensitive resources. Review the change set, backup state and rollback strategy before replacing production data infrastructure.

scenes.title: Infrastructure Composer in AWS Toolkit for VS Code
scenes.narration: This slide places Infrastructure Composer in a visual editing workflow for CloudFormation templates. The heading warns that the standalone console experience is ending on a stated date, so use the supported integration and verify current service availability rather than teaching the console as a permanent path. The workflow begins with a CloudFormation template opened in the AWS Toolkit for VS Code, then adds or connects resources on a canvas. The example shows an S3 document bucket, a Lambda processing function and a DynamoDB metadata table, alongside the corresponding YAML definitions. After editing, inspect the textual template diff; visual wiring is a convenience for authoring, not a substitute for reviewing IAM policies, properties or update risks. Finally deploy through CloudFormation and check stack events and outputs. The canvas describes desired infrastructure and does not provide live runtime observability. This matters because seeing a graphical connection between Lambda and DynamoDB does not prove the Lambda role has permission to write to that table. Treat the visual canvas as another way to author reviewable IaC.
